# Learning map and detailed syllabus {.unnumbered}

## The dependency structure

A chapter is self-contained in the sense that it defines its technical language
and reconstructs the tools used in its main argument. Self-contained does not
mean that every chapter reproves all of linear algebra. The first five chapters
establish reusable habits; later chapters briefly reintroduce the relevant
ingredients and link to fuller explanations.

| Stage | Questions | Mathematical tools developed | Evidence you should be able to produce |
|---|---|---|---|
| States and dynamics, chapters 1–5 | What is local information? What is actually evolving? | Partial trace, Schmidt decomposition, fermions, spectral sums, locality, exact computation | Compute a reduced state and a controlled finite-system quench |
| Thermalization and information, chapters 6–10 | Why do local observables relax? How is information hidden? | ETH, random matrices, entanglement quasiparticles, OTOCs, Haar moments, stabilizers | Separate spectral chaos, local equilibration, and scrambling |
| Conserved quantities, chapters 11–16 | What survives relaxation and controls late times? | Kubo formula, hydrodynamics, Bethe ansatz, thermodynamic dressing, GHD, dual unitarity | Derive and test a transport scaling law |
| Obstructions and driving, chapters 17–21 | How can memory persist or be stabilized? | Localization, resonances, avalanches, restricted spaces, Floquet expansions | Diagnose memory without mistaking a long transient for a phase |
| Baths and observation, chapters 22–26 | How does access to a measurement record change dynamics? | Channels, GKSL, trajectories, Liouvillian spectra, replicas, codes | Distinguish conditioned information from ensemble-averaged observables |
| Methods and frontiers, chapters 27–32 | Which assumptions remain valid in modern experiments and theories? | Critical scaling, kinetic and contour methods, constraints, estimators, MPS, research design | Reproduce a paper's central observable with quantified errors |

## Three suggested routes

**A first graduate course, 14 teaching weeks.** Spend weeks 1–3 on states,
models, quenches, and computation; weeks 4–5 on ETH, spectral chaos and
entanglement; weeks 6–7 on hydrodynamics and integrability; week 8 on localization
and its stability; week 9 on Floquet physics; weeks 10–11 on open and monitored
systems; week 12 on information and error correction; week 13 on tensor networks
and experiments; week 14 on student reproductions. Select exercises deeply
rather than trying to discuss every paper.

**Information dynamics route.** Read chapters 1, 3–5, 8–10, 22–26, 30–32.
Return to hydrodynamics when conservation produces slow purification or
nontrivial operator tails. A suitable first project compares trajectory entropy
with the entropy of the average state in the same finite circuit.

**Transport and ergodicity route.** Read chapters 1–7, 11–21, 28, 30–32.
Study entanglement before choosing a numerical method. A suitable first project
compares a conserved packet's second moment with the current autocorrelation,
then deliberately breaks integrability.

## Recurring models

The transverse-field Ising chain makes particles, criticality, quenches, and
Floquet resonances explicit. The XXZ chain connects symmetry, integrability,
transport, and anomalous dynamics. Random and exactly tractable circuits isolate
information spreading. Disordered spin chains expose resonances and finite-size
limitations. A damped two-level system introduces the distinction between a
density matrix and a trajectory. Rydberg-blockaded chains connect constraints to
experiments. Definitions and normalization conventions appear at each use.

## Competency checkpoints

1. Given a bipartite wavefunction, derive its reduced state, Schmidt values,
   entropy and mutual information. Explain why global purity permits local
   thermality.
2. Given a Hamiltonian, identify every symmetry used in a spectral calculation,
   distinguish degeneracies from accidental near crossings, and state the
   ordering of limits in a relaxation claim.
3. Starting from a microscopic continuity equation, derive a long-wavelength
   transport prediction and identify a measurement that can falsify it.
4. Explain when a generalized ensemble is needed, derive a simple dressing or
   free-particle transport equation, and distinguish ballistic quasiparticles
   from a diffusion correction.
5. Explain why a finite system with long memory does not prove stable MBL;
   estimate a resonance or heating scale and propose a competing explanation.
6. Derive both conditional and unconditional measurement evolution. Construct a
   reference-qubit diagnostic and explain its sampling cost.
7. Reproduce one observable, establish numerical convergence, locate an
   assumption in the original paper, and design an extension that tests it.

## What counts as completing an exercise?

A formula should come with its domain of validity, dimensions, and a limiting
check. A numerical answer should come with a model definition, convention,
system size, boundary condition, state or ensemble, timestep or truncation,
random seed, and at least one error check. An experimental interpretation should
specify which measured probability distribution supports the inferred quantity.
A research proposal should state what outcome would change your mind.

The full editorial architecture and per-chapter calculation targets are kept in
[research/OUTLINE.md](research/OUTLINE.md). The [research-paper map](research-map.qmd)
is the bridge from this syllabus to the original literature.
